Women live less long because of the chronic stress from men. Okay, there's a pretty major problem with this. One of the main claims here is simply wrong. And I'm not talking about some tiny technical disagreement between studies. The claim that married women generally die earlier than single women is basically the opposite of what some of the largest studies on the subject have found. Some of you may ask, well, why do I care so much about a bad statement in a podcast? Because this isn't some tiny podcast. Women of Impact has a huge audience. Lisa Bilyeu's YouTube channel alone has around 1.66 million subscribers and almost 200 million views. And this particular clip is pinned at the top of her Instagram. It has around 23 million views and more than half a million likes. And the man saying this isn't some random guy on TikTok. Daniel Amen is a double board certified psychiatrist, and a very prominent public figure in the mental health space. So when somebody with those credentials goes on a platform this big and confidently tells millions of people that married women die earlier because of chronic stress from men, I think it is worth checking whether that's actually true. And the evidence says, no, it is false. A 2020 meta-analysis combined 21 studies from 15 countries, almost 7.9 million people and nearly 1.9 million deaths. Compared with married women, unmarried women had a 22% higher risk of dying from any cause. And women who have never married, so probably the closest comparison to single women, had a 46% higher risk than married women. Then look at actual U.S. mortality data. In the CDC's final data for 2022, married women had an age-adjusted death rate of about 572 per 100,000. For women who had never married, 1,272. For divorced women, 1,184. And for widowed women, 1,655. So not only were married women not dying earlier, they had by far the lowest mortality rate. Now, there's an important caveat. None of this proves that getting married itself makes you live longer. Healthier people may be more likely to get married or stay married. Income, lifestyle, social support, and the quality of the marriage can all matter. But that caveat doesn't rescue their claim. Because they were not saying, we don't know whether marriage causes women to live longer. They were saying, married women probably die earlier. And the observed data go in the opposite direction. There is one thing they could have said that would have been fair. Men do appear to get a bigger mortality advantage from marriage than women do. In that same meta-analysis, unmarried men had a 46% higher mortality risk than married men, compared with 22% for women. So, men appear to benefit more from marriage? Support it. Married women probably die earlier? False. And women live less long because of chronic stress from men? An even stronger causal claim that the evidence does not establish. And this is what makes it so bad. A real finding gets twisted into blatant misinformation that to a certain extent paints men as the problem. Coming from one of America's most famous psychiatrists on a huge platform, millions will walk away believing that science has shown married women die earlier because men stress them out. But science has not shown that. The claim is false. And when you have this much authority and this much reach, spreading such misinformation is simply not okay.
